profile.reading:
Per a dedicated aggregator listing corroborated by CyrusOne's own SAT2-SAT4 campus page, this building (San Antonio III, inferred to correspond to SAT3 by sequential naming and campus grouping) sits at 9554 Westover Hills Boulevard, San Antonio, TX 78251 (one aggregator gave a minor house-number variant, 9500, not resolved further), on the shared 295,785 sq ft / 36MW SAT2-SAT4 campus.

CyrusOne's first San Antonio facility opened in 2012; per CyrusOne's own press release on its fifth San Antonio campus (SAT5-SAT6, broken ground January 2025 in Texas Research Park), the company had invested approximately $1 billion in capital to date across its San Antonio campuses as of that release, and describes SAT5-SAT6 itself as two buildings totaling 276,000 sq ft and 36 MW of IT capacity, figures that differ somewhat from an earlier operator-page-sourced figure of 175,000 sq ft/33 MW recorded for that campus elsewhere in this registry, a discrepancy noted rather than silently reconciled. The San Antonio Report, a local nonprofit newsroom, reported in 2026 that the city hosts more than 20 operational data centers with 59 more in various planning stages; CPS Energy, the municipally owned utility, supplies power to 21 of the existing facilities (generating roughly $110 million in revenue) and has projected future data center energy demand in the metro at approximately 26,000 megawatts, while flagging water use as a growing constraint: data centers currently draw about 0.1% of San Antonio Water System's drinking water, but planned new facilities have requested roughly 600 acre-feet of drinking water and 3,000 acre-feet of recycled water against a system that has capacity for only about 10,000 additional acre-feet before requiring upgrades.

CyrusOne's San Antonio growth mirrors a broader pattern across Texas, where absence of a state corporate income tax, relatively low land and construction costs compared to Northern Virginia or Silicon Valley, and CPS Energy's municipal-utility rate structure have made the metro attractive to colocation and hyperscale operators alike; San Antonio's data center footprint has grown alongside comparable buildouts in Dallas-Fort Worth (where CyrusOne's Carrollton facility, opened in 2012, was described by the company as the largest data center in Texas at the time) and Austin.

reading.body:
CyrusOne San Antonio III sits on the shared SAT2-SAT4 campus at 9554 Westover Hills Boulevard, occupying 295,785 square feet as one building within a three-building complex. The campus publishes 36 MW of total IT capacity across all three facilities combined, but the individual IT load for SAT3 is not published separately. At a conservative 40 kW per rack, the 36 MW campus-wide figure implies approximately 900 racks across SAT2-SAT4, though SAT3's share of that total cannot be determined from public data.

San Antonio hosts more than 20 operational data centers today with 59 more in planning stages, according to recent local reporting. CPS Energy, the municipal utility, supplies power to 21 existing facilities and has projected future metro data center demand at approximately 26,000 megawatts, a figure that dwarfs current deployed capacity. Water is the stated constraint: current data center operations draw 0.1% of San Antonio Water System's drinking water, but planned facilities have requested 600 acre-feet of drinking water and 3,000 acre-feet of recycled water against a system with roughly 10,000 acre-feet of additional capacity before requiring upgrades.

Texas publishes 468 MW of total data center IT capacity across 18 mapped facilities with public specifications, and SAT3 does not rank among the published capacity leaders in the state at rank 19. CyrusOne's San Antonio footprint reflects broader Texas trends: municipal utility pricing at CPS Energy, low land and construction costs, and state tax structure have drawn colocation and hyperscale investment to San Antonio alongside growth in Dallas-Fort Worth and Austin, but the metro's data center expansion is now upstream-constrained by water availability rather than power generation alone.
